subject: science
intro: Every material has properties we can observe or measure, such as color, hardness, texture, how well it conducts electricity, whether it is attracted to a magnet, whether it dissolves in water, how well it reflects light, and whether it floats. Different materials have different combinations of properties. By testing properties and comparing them in a table, we can tell materials apart and even identify an unknown material by matching its properties to a known one.

items.prompt: A student has an unknown metal. It is attracted to a magnet and conducts electricity. A property table shows iron is magnetic and conducts electricity, while aluminum conducts but is not magnetic. Which metal is it?

steps: List the tested properties: the metal is magnetic and conducts electricity.
Compare to the table: iron is magnetic and conducts; aluminum conducts but is not magnetic.
The sample is magnetic, so it matches iron, not aluminum.
solution.answer: Iron, because it is both magnetic and conducts electricity.

items.prompt: Three white powders look the same. Only one dissolves in water. How can the property of solubility help identify them?

steps: Looking alone is not enough because they share the same color and appearance.
Test each powder by stirring it into water and observing whether it dissolves.
The powder that dissolves has a different solubility property, so it can be told apart from the two that do not.
solution.answer: Testing solubility separates the one powder that dissolves from the two that do not.

items.prompt: A student wants to sort a mixed pile of materials into those that are attracted to a magnet and those that are not. What property is being used, and name one material in each group.

steps: The property being tested is magnetism: whether a material is attracted to a magnet.
Iron and steel paper clips are attracted to the magnet.
Plastic, wood, and aluminum are not attracted.
solution.answer: Magnetism. Example attracted: a steel paper clip. Example not attracted: a plastic button.

items.prompt: Why is color alone usually not enough to identify a material?

steps: Many different materials can share the same color.
To identify a material you need to test several properties, such as hardness, magnetism, and solubility, not just color.
solution.answer: Because many materials share the same color, so you must test more properties.

items.prompt: A sample floats in water, does not conduct electricity, and is soft enough to scratch with a fingernail. Is it more likely to be a metal or a piece of wood?

steps: Metals usually sink, conduct electricity, and are hard.
Wood often floats, does not conduct electricity, and can be soft.
The sample floats, does not conduct, and is soft, so it matches wood.
solution.answer: Wood, because it floats, does not conduct electricity, and is soft.

items.prompt: You need to measure the hardness of three materials to put them in order. Describe one fair way to compare their hardness.

steps: Hardness can be compared by seeing which material scratches another.
Try to scratch each material with the others under the same conditions.
A material that scratches the others but is not scratched itself is the hardest; order them from the one scratched most easily to the one scratched least.
solution.answer: Test which materials scratch the others; the one that scratches all others and is not scratched is hardest.
